ESTATE TAX EXEMPTION CALCULATOR · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER · NOTHING UPLOADED

Project your 2026 federal estate tax under the permanent $15M exclusion.

The One Big Beautiful Bill Act permanently set the federal estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer (GST) tax basic exclusion at $15,000,000 per person for 2026 — up to $30,000,000 for a married couple who elects portability. This tool applies that exclusion, any prior taxable gifts, and the flat 40% rate to your own numbers.

Nothing is uploaded. Your numbers are read in this browser and never leave your device — see the privacy note in the footer.

1. Filing situation

Choose "married" only if a Form 706 portability election was actually filed for a deceased spouse's estate. Being married alone does not add a second exclusion automatically.

2. Your numbers

Prior taxable gifts means amounts reported on Form 709 that exceeded the annual per-recipient exclusion ($19,000 in 2026) — not routine gifts within the annual exclusion, which never use up your lifetime exemption.

Fill in your filing situation and numbers, then click Calculate.

Projection

What this does not cover

  • Federal tax only. Several states impose their own estate or inheritance tax with thresholds far below $15,000,000, depending on the decedent's state of domicile — not modeled here.
  • No marital or charitable deduction. Property passing outright to a surviving spouse or to charity can reduce or defer estate tax beyond what this calculator shows — this tool projects exposure against the gross estate figure you supply, not a fully planned estate.
  • No valuation discounts. Discounts for minority interests or lack of marketability in closely held businesses or family entities are not modeled.
  • Not a Form 706 or Form 709. This is a planning estimate, not a filed return.

Common questions

What is the 2026 federal estate tax exemption?

The One Big Beautiful Bill Act permanently set the federal estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer tax basic exclusion amount at $15,000,000 per person starting January 1, 2026, with no scheduled expiration. A married couple can shield up to $30,000,000 combined if the surviving spouse elects portability of the first spouse's unused exclusion.

What is portability (DSUE)?

Portability lets a surviving spouse add a deceased spouse's unused exclusion (DSUE) to their own $15,000,000 exclusion, by timely filing Form 706 for the deceased spouse's estate and electing it — even if no estate tax was owed at that death. It is not automatic; the election has to be made.

Is the GST exemption portable too?

No. The generation-skipping transfer (GST) exemption was also raised to $15,000,000, but unlike the estate/gift exclusion, the GST exemption has never been portable between spouses. A deceased spouse's unused GST exemption cannot be added to a survivor's own.

Do lifetime gifts reduce my exemption at death?

Yes. Estate tax and gift tax share one unified lifetime exclusion. Taxable gifts made during life (amounts above the $19,000-per-recipient annual exclusion, reported on Form 709) reduce the exclusion that remains to shield your estate when you die.

Does this calculator include state estate tax?

No. This tool projects federal tax only. Several states impose their own estate or inheritance tax with thresholds far below $15,000,000, depending on the decedent's state of domicile — flagged as out of scope, not computed, since this tool has no reliable way to know your domicile.

Is this estate planning advice?

No. This calculator applies the published federal exclusion, portability, and tax-rate rules to the numbers you enter. It does not model the marital deduction, charitable deduction, valuation discounts, or state tax, and it is not a substitute for consulting a qualified estate planning attorney or CPA before you act.

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not legal, tax, or financial advice, and it does not replace a qualified estate planning attorney or CPA. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it, and for confirming your own numbers before filing Form 706 or Form 709. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you type, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record — nothing you enter is saved anywhere by this tool.

Everything runs in your browser. Your numbers are never uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors. Anonymous feature events (estimate_calculated, example_loaded) are counted only in local storage on your device. The counts can be deleted with the button below. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control are honoured.

Setting up a child's savings account too? See the Trump Account calculator — another new federal wealth-transfer provision, this one a $1,000 federal seed deposit for a newborn rather than the lifetime estate and gift exclusion.

Deciding whether to gift a house or shares now or let them pass at death? The gift vs inherit basis calculator prices the lost step-up in basis against the estate tax a gift can avoid.

Working this out by hand instead? See where a hand estimate of the 2026 estate tax exclusion usually goes wrong.

Free and open source. If this helped, the code is under an MIT licence — support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

This calculator vs. working out the 2026 estate tax exclusion by hand

The headline number is simple — $15,000,000 per person. The part that goes wrong by hand is portability, the GST trap, and whether last year's "sunset" warning still applies (it does not).

Where a hand estimate usually goes wrong

StepCommon mistake by handWhat this calculator does
Married exclusionAssumes marriage automatically doubles the exclusion to $30,000,000.Only adds a second $15,000,000 if a DSUE amount from an actual portability election is entered.
GST exemptionAssumes the GST exemption is portable between spouses like the estate/gift exclusion.Flags explicitly that the GST exemption has never been portable, even though it shares the same $15,000,000 figure.
Prior giftsTreats lifetime gifts and the estate exclusion as two separate buckets.Subtracts prior taxable gifts from the same unified exclusion before comparing it to the estate.
The 2025 sunset scareApplies an older article's warning that the exemption reverts to about $7,000,000 in 2026.Uses the permanent $15,000,000 OBBBA figure -- that sunset was cancelled, not merely delayed.
Is anything I enter uploaded anywhere?N/ANo. The calculator runs entirely in your browser; nothing is sent to a server.

Common questions

What's the single most common mistake working this out by hand?

Assuming a married couple automatically gets $30,000,000 just for being married. The second $15,000,000 only applies if a surviving spouse actually elects portability of a deceased spouse's unused exclusion (DSUE) by timely filing Form 706 -- it is not automatic.

What's the second most common mistake?

Assuming the generation-skipping transfer (GST) exemption is portable between spouses the same way the estate/gift exclusion is. It is not, and never has been -- a deceased spouse's unused GST exemption cannot be added to a survivor's own.

What arithmetic mistake gets made most often?

Forgetting that lifetime taxable gifts reduce the exclusion available at death. Estate and gift tax share one unified exclusion -- a taxable gift made years earlier uses up part of the same bucket that would otherwise shield the estate.

What sunset mistake gets made most often?

Relying on an older article warning that the exemption would revert to roughly $7,000,000 at the start of 2026. That sunset was real under prior law, but the One Big Beautiful Bill Act permanently cancelled it and set the 2026 exclusion at $15,000,000 instead, with no expiration date.

Does this calculator know my complete estate plan?

No. Neither this calculator nor a by-hand worksheet built from this page knows about a marital deduction, a charitable bequest, valuation discounts, or state estate tax. Both apply the same published federal exclusion, portability, and rate rules to the numbers you enter; verify against a qualified estate planning attorney or CPA before relying on either.

No warranty. This page and the linked calculator apply published federal estate, gift, and GST tax exclusion rules to numbers you supply. It is not legal, tax, or financial advice, and it does not replace a qualified estate planning attorney or CPA. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it, and for confirming your own numbers before filing Form 706 or Form 709.
